**Note:** You can use this file as you 'working document' where you can try out various investigation ideas and keep notes about your findings. How you use and structure this file is up to you. It is recommended that you keep notes about what you are investigating and what you find as this will make the process of creating your presentation and report easier. Please note that you _do not_ need to submit this file as part of your group project.



```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```


```{r load-lib, message = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
# Add any other libraries here

```

```{r load-data}
# load your data 
crime_data <- read.csv(
  "data/communities.data",
  header = FALSE,
  na.strings = "?",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
## Stage1  Dataset Structure
# Dataset dimensions
dim(crime_data)

# Number of observations
nrow(crime_data)

# Number of variables
ncol(crime_data)

# First six observations
head(crime_data[, 1:10])

# Variable types
table(sapply(crime_data, class))
```

```{r}
## Stage2 Investigate missing values
# Total number of missing values
sum(is.na(crime_data))
# Number of missing values in each variable
colSums(is.na(crime_data))
```
```{r}
## Stage 3 select relevant variables
crime_selected <- crime_data[, c(4, 128, 35, 18, 39, 38, 81)]
colnames(crime_selected) <- c(
  "Community",
  "ViolentCrime",
  "Poverty",
  "MedianHouseholdIncome",
  "Unemployment",
  "Education",
  "Housing"
)

head(crime_selected)
dim(crime_selected)

# Missing values in selected variables
colSums(is.na(crime_selected))

summary(crime_selected)
```
```{r}
## Stage4 Data Visualisation

library(tidyverse)

# Distribution of violent crime rates
ggplot(data = crime_selected,
       mapping = aes(x = ViolentCrime)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of violent crime rates",
    x = "Normalised violent crime rate",
    y = "Number of communities"
  )

```
this histogram shows a positively skewed distribution of normalised violent crime rates. Most communities have relatively low crime rate values, with the highest concentration occurring around 0.05. The frequency decreases as crime values increase. There are also some observations with particularly high crime values near 1. This suggests that there is variation in violent crime rates across communities, which we aim to investigate using socioeconomic variables.
